verdict: REGRESSION CONFIRMED, and it is a GENERALIZATION FAILURE rather than a new defect. Rule 2's anti-duplicate bullet (planner.py:32, shipped in 69d238f) did not fail because the model ignored it — it failed because on a Rule-3-shaped, non-Airtable two-step case the model is reading TWO other instructions that actively license a literal, and Rule 2's prohibition is the only one of the three that is (a) stated generically, (b) illustrated with a single Airtable-specific key (`table_name`), and (c) physically located in the clarification block, i.e. read AFTER the step's `parameters` object has already been composed. The two competing licenses are planner.py:38 (Rule 3's closing clause 'steps with no such dependency should keep concrete literal parameter values') — which fires on exactly this two-step handoff shape and never fires on srw-02 (single-step) — and planner.py:50 (Rule 5's carve-out, added in 71fb7b1) whose generalizing sentence 'The rule is: any name or value the user literally said belongs in `parameters` as a concrete literal' reads as a global principle and is satisfiable by the word 'orders', which the user DID literally say (as the DATA, not as the destination's name). fan-01/srw-02 hold because their winning instruction is the Rule 5 carve-out's point-of-use worked example; amb-02 has no such example to land on.
problem: The planner emits `spreadsheet_name` both in `missing_parameters` and as an invented literal inside step 2's `parameters` on 2 of 3 identical amb-02 runs at temperature 0.1 — a self-contradicting blueprint that, if the clarification is skipped or auto-answered, writes the user's order data into a Google Sheet named 'Orders' that the user never named. The same defect is present in a third form in the pre-fix baseline trace (`"spreadsheet_name": "{spreadsheet_name}"`), so the shipped Rule 2 amendment has changed the defect's spelling on this shape but not its incidence — Rule 2's fix generalizes to the two Airtable cases it was tuned against (fan-01, srw-02) and not to the Rule-3-shaped Google Sheets case.
evidence: planner.py:32 (worktree /private/tmp/voxagent-optimize-pass2/backend/app/services/planner.py) — the shipped anti-duplicate bullet, verbatim: "- If you add a parameter to `missing_parameters`, LEAVE THAT PARAMETER OUT of the step's `parameters` object entirely. Never do both — never list `table_name` as missing while also writing `\"table_name\": \"Invoices\"` into the step. ..." Its ONLY worked instance is `table_name` / "Invoices" — an Airtable key. No non-Airtable instance appears anywhere in Rule 2.

planner.py:36 (Rule 2, last bullet) — the ONLY place `spreadsheet_name` appears inside Rule 2 is the opaque-ID bullet: "(e.g. `parameter_key` \"spreadsheet_name\" with label \"Google Sheet Name\", not \"spreadsheet_id\")". So within Rule 2, `spreadsheet_name` is exemplified ONLY as a thing to PUT IN missing_parameters, and never as a thing to LEAVE OUT of parameters. The two bullets teach the two halves of the invariant with two different keys, and the model applied each half to the key it was demonstrated on: it correctly produced `parameter_key: "spreadsheet_name"` in missing_parameters (bullet 6's example) and did NOT transfer bullet 2's omission requirement (demonstrated on `table_name`).

planner.py:38 (Rule 3, closing sentence) — "Only use this when a step genuinely depends on another step's output; steps with no such dependency should keep concrete literal parameter values." amb-02 IS a Rule 3 case (step 2's `row_data` = `{step_1_result}`), so Rule 3 is in the model's active-attention set. Its closing clause partitions step 2's parameters into {dependent -> placeholder} and {non-dependent -> concrete literal}, with NO third bucket for 'flagged missing -> omit'. `spreadsheet_name` is non-dependent, so this clause reads as a direct instruction to give it a concrete literal. COMPETING INSTRUCTION, outside Rule 5, exactly as suspected.

planner.py:50 (Rule 5 carve-out, shipped in 71fb7b1) — "The rule is: any name or value the user literally said belongs in `parameters` as a concrete literal; only identities the user never gave at all are flagged as missing." The sentence opens with the globalizing phrase "The rule is:" and contains no fan-out qualifier, so it reads as a general principle even to a model that has not entered the fan-out branch. Its first clause is satisfiable by the token 'orders', which the amb-02 prompt literally contains — 'Grab the latest orders from our internal API'. The model appears to have used it to license `spreadsheet_name: "Orders"`. SECOND COMPETING INSTRUCTION, and it was introduced by the very fix that made fan-01 pass.

PLACEMENT ASYMMETRY — Rule 5's version of the invariant is at the POINT OF USE: it sits inside the sentence that instructs the model on what to write into `parameters` (planner.py:50, "Inside THIS step's `parameters`, ... IMPORTANT: do NOT invent a value for a constant parameter whose identity the user never gave"). Rule 2's version (planner.py:32) sits in the disambiguation block, which the model reaches when deciding to clarify — i.e. after step 2's parameters object has already been composed. Rule 2 never instructs a revisit, and nowhere in Rules 1-7 is there a final consistency check reconciling `missing_parameters` against `steps[].parameters`.

OBSERVED (pass2 live runs, gemini-3.1-flash-lite, temperature 0.1, prompt held constant, 3 repetitions): run 1 and run 2 both produced `missing_parameters=['spreadsheet_name']` AND step 2 `parameters = {'spreadsheet_name': 'Orders', 'row_data': '{step_1_result}', 'headers': [...]}`. Run 3 produced no duplicate. 2/3 duplicate rate on a non-fan-out, non-Airtable case, against a planner where fan-01/srw-02 are clean.

BASELINE (pre-fix), traces/planner-eval-traces.jsonl trace_id amb-02, output.blueprint.steps[1].parameters — `{"spreadsheet_name": "{spreadsheet_name}", "row_data": "{step_1_result}", "headers": ["Order ID", "Customer Name", "Total Amount", "Status"]}` with `missing_parameters[0].parameter_key == "spreadsheet_name"`. The duplicate KEY was present before the fix too, as a self-referential echo placeholder rather than an invented name. This matters twice over: (1) it shows the fix did not reduce incidence on this shape, and (2) Rule 2:32's prohibition is phrased against writing a plausible-looking VALUE ("A plausible-looking stand-in ... is indistinguishable from a value the user actually supplied"), which does not obviously cover an echo placeholder — so a model could satisfy Rule 2's stated reasoning while still emitting a duplicate key.

Tests that missing_parameters carries a per-step entry for each rather than clarifying only the first, and that neither a fake URL nor a fake sheet name is invented." The seed was authored to test exactly this, and it names the invented-sheet-name failure mode explicitly.

WHY fan-01/srw-02 DO hold (the contrast that isolates the cause): srw-02 is single-step, so Rule 3 never fires and its 'keep concrete literal parameter values' clause is never read. fan-01 is fan-out, so the model enters Rule 5 and lands on the point-of-use worked example "`base_name: \"Content Calendar\"` is a literal (user said it); `table_name` is missing (user never named the table inside that base)" — a fully worked instance of the exact decision being made, delivered at the moment the parameters object is written. amb-02 triggers NEITHER protection: Rule 3 fires (adding a competing license) and Rule 5 does not (removing the only point-of-use example).

secondaryObservations.possibleContributingCause: Rule 5 (planner.py:51) forbids adding a spurious `for_each` field but says nothing about using `{{item}}` outside a for_each step — the ban is on the wrong half of the pair. (1) The worked amb-02 example replaces the abstract 'every parameter' with a concrete non-Airtable instance whose parameters object is shown literally WITHOUT the key — the same delivery form that made Rule 5's carve-out stick on fan-01. (3) The FINAL CHECK bullet converts a memory-dependent constraint into a deterministic verification pass performed AFTER the JSON is composed, which is the point in the generation order where the defect actually occurs — this is the only part of the remedy that does not depend on the model recalling a rule at composition time.

2. In planner.py:38, replace the final sentence with the `after` text verbatim (doubled braces).
3. Mirror into agentspec.yaml:120 with single braces, and apply the companionSopEdit at agentspec.yaml:35.

4. Re-run amb-02 3x, then the full 24-trace regression. Watch specifically for over-correction on multi-step handoff traces that legitimately carry user-given literals in a downstream step — the risk is the model now under-populates a step whose destination the user DID name.
assumptions: Rule 3's closing clause is genuinely contributing rather than merely correlating with the two-step shape; this remains hypothesis-pending until the remedy-1-alone ablation is run.
Source access to planner.py and agentspec.yaml is available; both were read directly, so the `before` strings are byte-exact rather than inferred.

remedies.title: Add a repetition-based determinism guard so a 2-of-3 defect cannot pass as fixed
remedies.rationale: This regression was invisible to the existing harness for a structural reason: run_dataset_through_planner.py executes each seed ONCE, so a defect that fires on 2 of 3 identical runs has a 1-in-3 chance of being recorded as a clean pass. The three promoted fixes were validated against single runs of fan-01/srw-02, which is why a probabilistic residual survived promotion.
remedies.whyWorks: Running each clarification-relevant seed N=3 times and failing the criterion if ANY repetition contradicts turns a sampled observation into a bound. It also makes the remedy-1 A/B bar in step 5 above (3/3 clean) mechanically enforced rather than a manual convention.
remedies.describedChange: Extend run_dataset_through_planner.py with a `--repeat N` flag (default 1, use 3 for the ambiguous-recipient-or-target and fan-out-batch scenarios) that emits one trace per repetition with a `repetition` field in metadata; then extend the clause-2 duplicate-key check in tier0_code_checks.py's check_no_guessed_required_param to aggregate across repetitions of the same trace_id and return fail if ANY repetition contains a parameter_key present in both missing_parameters and the matching step's parameters, reporting the k/N incidence in the note. Cost is a 3x Gemini spend on the affected scenarios only, not the whole 24-trace set.
applyInstructions: 1. Add the `--repeat N` flag to run_dataset_through_planner.py, tagging each emitted trace with metadata.repetition.
2. In tier0_code_checks.py, group verdicts by trace_id base and fail the clause-2 duplicate check if any repetition contradicts; include the k/N rate in the note.
3. Re-baseline before applying remedy 1 so the pre-fix incidence (expected 2/3 on amb-02) is on record, then re-run after.
4. Extend to fan-01/srw-02/amb-01/amb-03 so the promoted fixes get the same determinism bound they were never held to.
assumptions: The harness scripts are editable and re-runnable in this environment; both were located but not executed as part of this analysis.
A 3x repetition is enough to catch a ~2/3-incidence defect with acceptable confidence; a genuinely rare (<10%) residual would still slip through.
